title: A few months of building a BTC 5/15-minute Polymarket bot (Part 1/2)
author: Orphis_
selftext:
**TL;DR:** I started building a bot for Polymarket's short-duration BTC markets thinking the interesting problem would be predicting Bitcoin. A few months later, most of my time was going into stale-data handling, execution checks, logging, failures, and figuring out whether the strategy or the infrastructure was actually responsible for a result. The bot eventually became **Orphis**.  
.

.

.

I've been working on this project on and off for a few months and figured I'd write down the whole thing before I stop working on it.

It started as a pretty basic idea.

Polymarket has short-duration BTC markets, and I wanted to see if I could build something that watched BTC, watched the prediction market, generated its own estimate, and acted when there was enough of a difference between the two.

The first version in my head was basically:

`BTC data -> signal -> compare with Polymarket -> trade`

I started with the **5-minute markets**, later spent more time around the **15-minute markets**, and eventually started calling the project **Orphis**.

At the beginning I spent most of my time thinking about the signal itself.

What recent BTC movement should matter? How much should momentum matter? How should the model behave as the market gets closer to expiry? Is there ever enough of a lag between the underlying market and the prediction-market price to do something useful with it?

I assumed that was going to be most of the project.

It wasn't.

# The first thing that caused problems was data

Getting a BTC price is obviously easy.

Knowing whether the BTC price your program is looking at is actually safe to make a decision with is a different problem.

On a 5 or 15-minute market, a few seconds can actually matter.

I started running into situations where one source had updated and another hadn't, requests took longer than expected, connections briefly dropped, or an API technically returned successfully but the information wasn't as fresh as I expected.

None of this is particularly exotic, but I hadn't really thought about it when I started.

So more and more checks started appearing.

**When did I receive this?**

**How old is it?**

**How long did the request take?**

**Do the timestamps across the different inputs make sense?**

**Has anything stalled?**

Eventually I had explicit rules where a signal could look perfectly fine and the system would still refuse to do anything because it didn't trust the state of the data.

That was probably the first big change in how I thought about the bot.

A lot of the work wasn't going to be figuring out when to trade.

It was figuring out when **not** to trade.

# Execution turned into a separate system too

The early versions were conceptually very close to:

`signal = good -> send order`

I stopped being comfortable with that fairly quickly.

Even if the strategy produces a valid signal, a bunch of other things can change before an order should actually be sent.

The market can move.

The input can go stale.

There may not be enough time remaining.

One of the feeds might be unhealthy.

The state of the Polymarket market itself might have changed.

So I separated the strategy from execution.

The strategy could say:

>*I would take this.*

And then a separate set of checks could still say:

>*No.*

That separation ended up becoming one of the more important parts of the system.

By this point, Orphis was slowly becoming less of a Python script and more of a collection of small systems that all had to agree with each other.

# Then I realized I wasn't recording enough

This became obvious the first few times I tried to understand a bad result.

Say a trade loses.

The easiest conclusion is:

*the signal was wrong.*

But was it?

Maybe the signal was bad.

Maybe the underlying data was old.

Maybe the market moved between signal generation and execution.

Maybe there was unusual latency.

Maybe one threshold only barely passed.

Maybe the execution logic did something I didn't expect.

And then there was the opposite situation: something gets rejected, I check later, and it would have been profitable.

Again, it's easy to say:

*the filter was wrong.*

But the fact that a trade worked afterward doesn't mean the system was wrong to reject it with the information it had at the time.

I needed to be able to reconstruct what the bot actually knew.

So I started storing a lot more.

Signals, observations, timestamps, decisions, rejection reasons, execution information, diagnostics, results.

I used **SQLite** for most of this.

That was probably one of the biggest improvements I made, even though it had nothing to do with predicting BTC.

Before that, debugging a losing trade was often:

>*Something went wrong. Maybe change the strategy.*

Afterward it became:

>*What exactly happened here?*

Sometimes the answer really was that the signal sucked.

Other times it wasn't.

# Rejected trades became interesting too

Eventually I started spending a surprising amount of time looking at things Orphis **didn't** do.

Signals that got close to the threshold.

Trades that passed the strategy but failed an execution check.

Trades rejected because something wasn't fresh enough.

Situations where one filter prevented execution.

Those started to matter because just looking at completed trades gives you a pretty distorted view of the system.

If you tighten a filter and your win rate goes up, that sounds good.

But what did you remove?

Did the filter genuinely eliminate bad setups, or did it just reduce the sample?

How many good opportunities did it remove at the same time?

Was the strategy wrong, or was the execution layer too conservative?

I hadn't really appreciated how important that distinction was before building this.

# Things also just... break

Another thing that took me longer than it should have to accept:

APIs fail.

Connections drop.

Requests time out.

Feeds stall.

Unexpected values appear.

At first every one of those felt like a bug I needed to somehow prevent from ever happening again.

Eventually the design changed to assuming failures **will** happen.

Then the problem becomes:

**Does the system notice?**

and

**What does it do next?**

That led to retry logic, recovery paths, more diagnostics, safe states, and a lot more reasons for the execution layer to simply refuse a trade.

That work isn't very exciting to show someone, but it made the bot feel much more real than adding another indicator ever did.

# The strategy itself was still changing the entire time

This part was much less clean.

I'd change something and get a promising set of results.

Then I'd collect more observations and it wouldn't look as impressive anymore.

I'd adjust something else.

Sometimes that genuinely helped.

Sometimes I had just fitted something to the data I already had.

Sometimes I'd change part of the strategy and accidentally expose a completely unrelated problem somewhere else.

There were periods where I thought I was getting somewhere and periods where I seriously wondered why I was spending so much time on it.

I never had a single moment where everything suddenly clicked and the bot became great.

It was much more incremental than that.

But somewhere during all of this, what started as my **BTC 5min / BTC 15min bot** became Orphis.

It now had data collection, signal generation, persistence, execution gating, failure handling, diagnostics, and analysis around both completed and rejected decisions.

The funny part is that when I started, the part I cared about was the model.

By this point, the part I found more interesting was everything around it.

**Part 2 is about what happened when I started trying to work out whether I could actually trust the results, some mistakes I made along the way, where the project eventually ended up, and why I'm stopping it now.**

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
The line about not being able to tell whether the strategy or the infrastructure was responsible is the real finding here, and it is the part nobody warns you about before you start.

What helped us most was making those two failure classes structurally different instead of trying to separate them after the fact. Every order gets a decision record written before it goes out: what the signal said, what price we expected, and how old each input was at that instant. The fill then gets compared against that record rather than against a backtest. Right decision plus bad fill is infra. Bad decision is the strategy. The argument stops because the record already answered it.

The stale data handling is that same problem wearing a different hat. A bar four seconds old and a bar four minutes old are not the same input, but most systems hand them to the strategy identically. Stamping input age onto every decision turned a whole category of mystery losses into one data source lagging at a particular time of day.

replies.author: masatumas
replies.body: Agree. Stale data, unstable connection are some of the biggest failure rates. Experienced the same.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: Stale data is the sneakier of the two, since nothing errors out. The bot just acts on a price that already moved. We timestamp every input and refuse the order if any leg is older than a threshold.

comments.author: masatumas
comments.body: Hey. I experienced the same of what you shared when I started building mine in April. I am curious, what is the thesis that you’re generating your thesis on?
